pack.title: Setting boundaries early
pack.description: New-dating pressure tests. Clear early beats resentful later.

scenarios.setting: Third date. You say you have an early morning; they order another round.
scenarios.jab: Oh come on, one more. Don't be boring.

replies.line: I'm good — and boring is underrated. See you next week.
replies.why: Owning the label removes its sting and your exit keeps your morning intact.
It skips the debate entirely — leaving is the boundary, stated once.

replies.line: Next time I'll close the place down. Tonight I need my sleep.
replies.why: A promise of future fun softens a present no without weakening it.

replies.line: Boring people need sleep too. It's in the handbook.
replies.why: Agreeing with the charge at double volume turns it into a shared joke.
It signs the label and exits on schedule, which is the whole point.

trap.line: Fine, ONE more, but you're annoying.
trap.why: Caving with resentment teaches them pressure works and you keep score.

scenarios.setting: Two weeks in. They want your location shared, always.
scenarios.jab: If you have nothing to hide, just share your location. Everyone does it.

replies.line: I don't share that this early. Trust builds first.
replies.why: It states your timeline as policy, which makes it about pacing, not hiding.
A clean no with a door left open — the pressure has nowhere to grip.

replies.line: I'm not there yet — let's earn the boring-couple perks first.
replies.why: Framing privacy as a stage of the relationship keeps it warm and firm.

replies.line: My location's shy. It needs time.
replies.why: Giving your phone stage fright keeps the boundary cute instead of cold.

replies.line: Hidden? No. Just not yours yet.
replies.why: It corrects secrecy framing into pacing, which is the actual truth.
